title: Job 1:1–5
context: The narrator opens the book with Job in the land of Uz: a man “blameless and upright,” who feared God and turned away from evil, blessed with seven sons and three daughters, great flocks, and a very great household, “the greatest of all the children of the east.” Job’s children feast in turn, and Job continually offers burnt offerings for them, lest they have sinned and “renounced God in their hearts.” The speaker of this unit is the narrator, with Job’s own words quoted in 1:5. Uz’s location is not fixed here; proposals often look east of the Jordan or toward Edom, but they remain uncertain. The book also does not date Job’s life. Later Scripture treats him as a real righteous man, named with Noah and Daniel in Ezekiel 14:14 and remembered in James 5:11; those witnesses may be named without turning this prologue into a chronology. The unit is an introduction to Job’s piety and prosperity, not a coded lesson in the numbers. Both traditions take the narrator’s portrait as the standing against which the coming test will be measured, without a contrast over the site or the era.

verses.text: There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job. That man was blameless and upright, and one who feared God, and turned away from evil.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator begins, “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job.” Job is “blameless and upright, and one who feared God, and turned away from evil.” The praise is moral and religious together: integrity, fear of God, and a turning from evil. Uz is named and not located; common suggestions place it in the east, sometimes near Edom, but the site is uncertain and should be left open. The book does not date his life.

Arminian readers take the opening as a real portrait of a historical man whose fear of God and turning from evil are genuine, the ground of the story that follows.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also receive the narrator’s judgment as the book’s own introduction, a blameless and upright man, not a stock figure invented only to raise a question. Ezekiel 14:14 will later name Job with Noah and Daniel among the righteous; that later witness agrees with this first line without fixing the era.

Both traditions keep Uz and the date hedged, and they invent no contrast over the geography or the timing.

verses.text: There were born to him seven sons and three daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
“There were born to him seven sons and three daughters.” The narrator counts the children before the wealth, a household already full. The numbers will matter when the losses come; here they are simply the family God has given him, reported without a symbolic decoding of seven and three.

Arminian readers take the ten children as a real family, the first and dearest part of Job’s prosperity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a historical household, seven sons and three daughters, named as born to him, not as a coded set of figures.

Both traditions refuse to allegorize the count, and they hold the children in view with pastoral restraint, knowing what the chapter will later tell.

verses.text: His possessions also were seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, five hundred female donkeys, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the children of the east.
verses.arminianNotes:
His possessions are listed in full: seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, five hundred female donkeys, “and a very great household”; so that “this man was the greatest of all the children of the east.” The greatness is public and material, set in the east, consistent with a life outside Israel’s later map, though that is not a dating of the book by itself.

Arminian readers take the inventory as a real measure of standing, a greatness the coming losses will touch in detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the narrator measuring Job among the children of the east, blessed in herd and household, without turning the totals into a hidden scheme.

Both traditions keep the wealth as the narrator states it, the setting for the charge that Job fears God only because of a hedge around all he has.

verses.text: His sons went and held a feast in the house of each one on his birthday; and they sent and called for their three sisters to eat and to drink with them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The sons hold a feast in the house of each one on his birthday, and they send for their three sisters to eat and drink with them. The narrator describes a regular, shared joy in the family, not a scene of already proven sin. The feasts will be the occasion of the last report in the chapter; here they are simply the children’s custom.

Arminian readers take the birthday feasts as a real family practice, brothers and sisters together, reported without suspicion the narrator has not raised.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the feasts as the text gives them, a rotating hospitality, not a hidden indictment of the household.

Both traditions refuse to read guilt into the meals in advance, and they invent no contrast over the custom.

verses.text: It was so, when the days of their feasting had run their course, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all. For Job said, “It may be that my sons have sinned, and renounced God in their hearts.” Job did so continually.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the days of feasting have run their course, Job sends and sanctifies them, rises early, and offers burnt offerings “according to the number of them all.” Job’s own words, given by the narrator, are, “It may be that my sons have sinned, and renounced God in their hearts.” Job does so continually. The offerings are Job’s priestly care for a possible inward sin he does not claim to have seen. The speaker of the quoted sentence is Job.

Arminian readers hear a genuine, habitual piety: he intercedes for his children on the chance they have sinned, a free and continual act of fear of God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the continual offerings as the narrator’s exhibit of Job’s uprightness, already matching 1:1. The words “It may be” keep the sin hypothetical; the children are not here charged.

Both traditions read the verse as the close of the portrait, Job’s care for his household before God, not as proof that the sons had already renounced God.
